title: Episode 2 (lines 354–548)

teacherSummary.text: The Guard brings in Antigone, caught performing the rites again. She admits the act and defends it: Creon's edict cannot override the unwritten laws of the gods. Creon condemns her. Ismene tries to share the blame; Antigone refuses her. Creon orders both sisters held.

context.history: Antigone appeals to divine, unwritten law; Creon to the authority of the State. Hegel reads the play as a collision of two powers: Antigone reverences the ties of blood and the gods below, while Creon recognizes Zeus as the power of public life (Hegel, 1838/1920, sec. "The Concrete Development of Dramatic Poetry and its Types").

significance: Two stubborn wills meet. Creon's fear that "I am woman, she the man" (lines 449–450) shows that his anger is also about gender and power.
discussionQuestions: Are there laws higher than a government's laws? Who decides what they are?
Where does characterization appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with learning too late?

satQuestions.passage:
At last it ceased, and lo! there stood this maid.
A piercing cry she uttered, sad and shrill,
As when the mother bird beholds her nest
Robbed of its nestlings; even so the maid
Wailed as she saw the body stripped and bare,
And cursed the ruffians who had done this deed.
Anon she gathered handfuls of dry dust,
Then, holding high a well-wrought brazen urn,
Thrice on the dead she poured a lustral stream.
We at the sight swooped down on her and seized
Our quarry. Undismayed she stood, and when
We taxed her with the former crime and this,
She disowned nothing. I was glad—and grieved;
For ’tis most sweet to ’scape oneself scot-free,
And yet to bring disaster to a friend
Is grievous. Take it all in all, I deem
A man’s first duty is to serve himself.

anchorPassages.note: Teaching hinge: human edict cannot override Zeus and the unwritten laws that do not die.
anchorPassages.text:
Guilty. I did it, I deny it not.
Sirrah, begone whither thou wilt, and thank
Thy luck that thou hast ’scaped a heavy charge.
Now answer this plain question, yes or no,
Wast thou acquainted with the interdict?
I knew, all knew; how should I fail to know?
And yet wert bold enough to break the law?
Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus,
And she who sits enthroned with gods below,
Justice, enacted not these human laws.
Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man,
Could’st by a breath annul and override
The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.
They were not born today nor yesterday;
They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang.

locator.opening: Guilty. I did it, I deny it not.
locator.closing: die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang.
locator.landmark: Antigone confesses and invokes Justice and the immutable unwritten laws of Heaven

anchorPassages.note: Gendered authority: Creon stakes manhood on punishing the proud girl who flouts him.
anchorPassages.text:
But this proud girl, in insolence well-schooled,
First overstepped the established law, and then—
A second and worse act of insolence—
She boasts and glories in her wickedness.
Now if she thus can flout authority
Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
But though she be my sister’s child or nearer
Of kin than all who worship at my hearth,
Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape
The utmost penalty, for both I hold,
As arch-conspirators, of equal guilt.

locator.opening: But this proud girl, in insolence well-schooled,
locator.landmark: Creon: the stubborn will bends like over-heated iron; he will not be woman to her man

anchorPassages.note: Mutual love vs civic hate: she buries a brother; he refuses to make a foe a friend even in death.
anchorPassages.text:
And yet how otherwise had I achieved
A name so glorious as by burying
A brother? so my townsmen all would say,
Were they not gagged by terror. Manifold
A king’s prerogatives, and not the least
That all his acts and all his words are law.
Of all these Thebans none so deems but thou.
These think as I, but bate their breath to thee.
Hast thou no shame to differ from all these?
To reverence kith and kin can bring no shame.
Was his dead foeman not thy kinsman too?
One mother bare them and the self-same sire.
Why cast a slur on one by honouring one?
The dead man will not bear thee out in this.
Surely, if good and evil fare alike.
The slain man was no villain but a brother.
The patriot perished by the outlaw’s brand.
Nathless the realms below these rites require.
Not that the base should fare as do the brave.
Who knows if this world’s crimes are virtues there?
Not even death can make a foe a friend.
My nature is for mutual love, not hate.

locator.opening: And yet how otherwise had I achieved
locator.closing: My nature is for mutual love, not hate.
locator.landmark: Antigone vs Creon on love, hate, and whether the dead foe was still kin

anchorPassages.note: Ismene's late courage meets Antigone's hard purity: partnership refused once cannot be claimed now.
anchorPassages.text:
I did the deed, if she will have it so,
And with my sister claim to share the guilt.
That were unjust. Thou would’st not act with me
At first, and I refused thy partnership.
But now thy bark is stranded, I am bold
To claim my share as partner in the loss.
Who did the deed the under-world knows well:
A friend in word is never friend of mine.
O sister, scorn me not, let me but share
Thy work of piety, and with thee die.
Claim not a work in which thou hadst no hand;
One death sufficeth. Wherefore should’st thou die?

locator.opening: I did the deed, if she will have
locator.closing: One death sufficeth. Wherefore should’st thou die?
locator.landmark: Ismene claims share in the deed; Antigone refuses a friend in word only

anchorPassages.note: Family and marriage enter the sentence: Creon chooses the State over his son's betrothal.
anchorPassages.text:
What wilt thou slay thy own son’s plighted bride?
Aye, let him raise him seed from other fields.
No new espousal can be like the old.
A plague on trulls who court and woo our sons.
O Haemon, how thy sire dishonours thee!
A plague on thee and thy accursed bride!
What, wilt thou rob thine own son of his bride?
’Tis death that bars this marriage, not his sire.
So her death-warrant, it would seem, is sealed.
By you, as first by me; off with them, guards,
And keep them close. Henceforward let them learn
To live as women use, not roam at large.

weDoAnswers: Antigone appeals to divine, unwritten law; Creon to the authority of the State. Hegel reads the play as a collision of two powers: Antigone reverences the ties of blood and the gods below, while Creon recognizes Zeus as the power of public life (Hegel, 1838/1920, sec. "The Concrete Development of Dramatic Poetry and its Types"). Read closely: “Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus, And she who sits enthroned with gods below, Justice, enacted not these human laws. Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man, Could’st by a breath annul and override The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang.” (Antigone, lines 417–424).
analysis.weDoWords: “Unwritten”, “immutable” and “mortal man” stand out in lines 417–424. Antigone sets laws that never change against the order of one human ruler, so she argues that the gods’ law outranks Creon’s. “By a breath annul” makes his edict sound slight beside laws no mortal can override.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Guilty. I did it, I deny it not” slowly and put it in my own words: Antigone admits the burial at once and refuses to hide or soften what she has done. Next, craft. The three short clauses—“Guilty,” “I did it,” “I deny it not”—leave no room for plea or excuse; the wording is open and defiant in a single breath. The strongest word is “Guilty”: it is the first word, and it admits the deed without a plea. Then, effect. What does line 410 reveal about Antigone before Creon? My answer: Two stubborn wills meet here. Antigone’s admission stands before Creon without excuse, and Creon's later fear that “I am woman, she the man” (lines 449–450) shows that his anger is also about gender and power, not only about the law.
